Monmouth County layout

Monmouth County occupies the central coast of New Jersey, bordered by Middlesex and Mercer Counties to the west, Ocean County to the south, the Atlantic Ocean to the east and Raritan Bay to the north. Of 661.40 square miles, only 468.18 are land, because 29.2% of the area is water. Freehold Borough is the county seat, and the county holds fifty-three municipalities.

The shore towns, from Long Branch and Asbury Park down to Spring Lake, set the market for oceanfront homes, while western towns such as Freehold, Marlboro and Colts Neck are inland and more rural. Middletown Township is the most populous municipality, with 67,106 residents in 2020, and Howell Township is the largest by area at 61.21 square miles.

Who handles property tax

Municipal offices send the bills. Each of the county's towns has its own assessor and tax collector, and the Monmouth County Board of Taxation oversees assessments and hears appeals. The board sits at the Hall of Records, 1 East Main Street, Freehold, NJ 07728, and its phone number is (732) 431-7404.

  • Five members are appointed by the governor.
  • The board hears assessment disputes, and the municipality is represented by its attorney.
  • All of its meetings are public.

The county also offers a property tax estimator through its record search, which owners can use to project a bill.

For a payoff before closing, call the collector for the town where the house stands. Your title company will ask that town's tax office for the figure.

The January 15 appeal calendar

Monmouth follows an alternate assessment calendar, and the tax appeal deadline is January 15 rather than April 1. Burlington and Gloucester counties are on the same calendar. Hearings are generally held after the January 15 deadline, and the board generally denies adjournments.

What the board expects from you:

  • The board starts from the view that your assessment is right, and you must show it is excessive or discriminatory.
  • Tie your evidence to the October 1 assessment date. If comparable sales did not go in with the petition, send at least three to the assessor, the clerk and the tax board a week ahead of the hearing.
  • Keep every tax and municipal charge current through the first quarter, paid to the collector.
  • Income-producing property needs an income statement on the board's own forms.
  • Miss the hearing and the case is dismissed for lack of prosecution.

If the result disappoints you, the Tax Court of New Jersey takes an appeal filed within 45 days of the mailing of the judgment. An assessment above $1,000,000 can skip the county board and go straight to the Tax Court by April 1. The Chapter 123 test also applies: when the ratio of assessment to true value exceeds the average ratio by more than 15%, the assessment is reduced to the common level.

Annual reassessment in Monmouth County

Monmouth took part in an Assessment Demonstration Program created by P.L. 2013, c. 15, which moved the county toward more frequent reassessment. A university study found that inequity in residential assessments dropped after the program began, and the county's assessors association and tax board received a 2019 Distinguished Jurisdiction Award from the International Association of Assessing Officers.

For owners, values are updated more often, so a change in the assessment notice reflects recent sales instead of waiting for a one-time revaluation. Middletown's aggregate preliminary net value for tax year 2026 was 7.94% above 2025, and the rate was expected to fall as a result. You can look up property record cards, sales data and prior postcards in the county's online record search before deciding to appeal.

Monmouth County home values

Monmouth is a wealthy, owner-heavy county, and with more than a fifth of residents over 65 it sees plenty of sales by longtime owners, heirs and downsizers.

Hurricane Sandy in 2012 hit the northern Jersey Shore hard, and whole neighborhoods in Monmouth County were demolished and rebuilt, some at a higher price level than before. For a seller, a location on the water or near a train line sets much of the price, and the assessor's record for your lot sets the tax.

Relief programs

Statewide relief reaches Monmouth owners too. Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ are paid for by the fiscal year 2027 budget and each has a yearly application window, so look on the Division of Taxation relief page for the next one. Local assessors handle the senior, disabled and veteran deductions on the municipal side, and many offices will also review a property record card with you.

A sale during the year may change eligibility, so ask the state program office how a mid-year move affects a claim before you close.

Selling in Monmouth County with a tax balance

Your town's collector issues the payoff, not the county, and the closing agent pays it out of your proceeds. Get the number in writing with interest figured to the closing date. Mid-appeal, taxes and municipal charges through the first quarter still have to be current. A cash purchase skips the lender's steps, but the tax payoff and deed recording are the same, so open the conversation with the collector early.

The order of work is simple. First, find the block and lot on your tax bill or in the county record search. Second, call the collector for the balance by quarter and ask whether any lien sits on the parcel. Third, if you think the assessment is too high, mark January 15 on the calendar, because that is the date the board must have your petition. Fourth, hand the written payoff to the title company a few days before the closing.

Heirs and downsizers often sell a house that has been in the family for decades. If you are in that position, ask the assessor whether an old deduction is still on the account, and bring the paperwork that shows you now own the house. Buyers and their lenders look at the tax on record when they estimate monthly costs, so a stale deduction or a pending appeal can change what they offer. Settle those questions before the listing goes live rather than after you have a contract.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Monmouth County property tax appeal deadline?

January 15. Monmouth uses an alternate assessment calendar, and the statewide April 1 date does not apply to most owners. An assessment over $1,000,000 can go directly to the Tax Court by April 1.

How do I contact the Monmouth County Board of Taxation?

Call (732) 431-7404 or write to the County Board of Taxation, Hall of Records, 1 East Main Street, Freehold, NJ 07728. The board can send the forms needed to file an assessment appeal.

What if I disagree with the Monmouth County Tax Board's decision?

You have 45 days from the date the judgment was mailed to file a further appeal with the Tax Court of New Jersey. Missing a hearing leads to dismissal for lack of prosecution, which can block that next step.

Can I appeal my Monmouth County property tax bill itself?

No. Taxes come from local budgets and cannot be appealed. You can challenge only the assessment, and you must pay all taxes and municipal charges through the first quarter while the appeal is pending.

How many comparable sales do I need for a Monmouth County appeal?

Submit at least three comparable sales. The board wants them delivered to the assessor, the clerk and the tax board at least a week before the hearing if they were not attached to the petition.

Who sends the property tax bill in Bergen County

Your town does. Bergen County is split into 70 municipalities (56 boroughs, nine townships, three cities and two villages), more than any other New Jersey county, and each one assesses its own parcels and collects its own tax. The county has one tax body, the Bergen County Board of Taxation, which sits at Two Bergen County Plaza, 1st Floor, Hackensack, and takes assessment appeals. Its number is 201-336-6300. The county website also hosts a property record search and the board's meeting schedule.

Oakland and Mahwah fall inside the Highlands preservation area, where extra state rules from a 2004 water protection law apply. A seller there should ask the town what limits a buyer might face.

The Bergen County housing market

Bergen has the largest population of any New Jersey county, with an estimated 977,026 people in 2025. It is a costly, owner-heavy market.

  • Half of owned homes are worth more than $623,000.
  • The middle household earns $124,884 a year.
  • Owners occupy 65.3 percent of households.
  • Owners with a mortgage pay a median $3,547 a month, and those without pay $1,498.
  • Rent runs $1,914 a month.

The county holds the northern ends of the New Jersey Turnpike and Garden State Parkway, the eastern end of Interstate 80 and a stretch of Interstate 287, and the George Washington Bridge ties Fort Lee to Upper Manhattan. The mean commute is 31.2 minutes, so access to highways and buses is part of how a house gets priced.

Appeal deadlines and filing steps

Petitions go to the Bergen County Board of Taxation, which asks filers to use its online system. The cutoff is April 1, or 45 days after bulk assessment notices go out, and moves to May 1 when a town has revalued. Mark the date each spring, because a late petition is not heard.

What proof helps at a hearing

The state wants market value on the October 1 valuation date, supported by sales that closed before that day. Assessments of similar houses are not accepted as proof.

  • Three to five recent sales of homes like yours.
  • Photos of your house and each comparable.
  • An income statement, for commercial property.
  • An appraisal or repair estimate where the house has flaws.

Attend the hearing. The board rarely grants delays, and missing it can produce a judgment for lack of prosecution that closes the door on the Tax Court of New Jersey. Where a town has not revalued lately, the board also measures your assessment against a band of 15 percent either side of the district's average ratio.

Taxes before closing

Request a payoff from your town's tax collector, not the county. The title company or closing attorney wants to know which quarterly installments are paid and what interest is owed. Quarters commonly fall on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, and your own collector will confirm local dates.

  • Ask your attorney how the contract splits the quarter in which you close.
  • Report any addition you built, since added assessments can create an extra bill.
  • If an appeal is still pending, decide in the contract who gets any refund.

Back taxes and interest are paid out of the seller's share at closing, so get the payoff figure before you fix a closing date. A balance that is a quarter or two behind does not stop a sale. It only changes the number on the settlement statement.

Senior and disabled owner deduction

Older residents and disabled owners may qualify for a $250 deduction through Form PTD, renewed each year with Form PD5 by March 1. The Division of Taxation's Property Administration unit takes questions at 609-292-7974 or 609-292-7975. If you hold the deduction and you are selling mid-year, tell your closing agent so the proration is based on the right amount.

Selling when time matters

Some Bergen County owners cannot wait for a listing, an appraisal and a buyer's mortgage. An inherited house, a pending move or a stack of tax notices can make a firm date worth more than a top price. In a cash sale, the buyer skips financing and takes the house as-is, so repairs and showings drop away.

The tax work does not disappear. Order a collector payoff, check for open permits or unreported additions, and sort out who gets any appeal refund. Those three steps cover most of the questions a title company will ask.

Steps to take before you list

Start with three calls. Ask your town's tax collector for a payoff and the dates of your quarterly installments. Ask the assessor for your property record card and compare it with the house as it stands today. Then ask the Board of Taxation whether your town has revalued recently, since that decides whether your petition date is April 1 or May 1.

With those answers you can decide whether an appeal is worth filing before you sell or whether the closing date matters more. A pending appeal can be carried into a sale, as long as the contract says who receives any refund.

What happens on hearing day

Bring the same packet you filed: three to five comparable sales, photos and any appraisal or repair estimate. The board looks at what the house was worth on the October 1 valuation date, not at what the neighbors pay in tax. Copies of your evidence must reach the assessor and the board seven days ahead, so build that into your schedule.

A decision is due within three months of the petition deadline. If the board lowers your value, the new figure is frozen for the appeal year and the two years after it, unless something such as a revaluation changes it. If you lose, the Tax Court of New Jersey is the next step, and a missed hearing can end that option.

Reading your assessment notice

The notice lists the assessed value for the land and the buildings. Check the lot size, the square footage, the number of rooms and any finished basement against what you own. A simple error on the record card is one of the easiest ways to win a reduction. Photos of damage, a failing roof or a flooded basement help show that the house is worth less than the card assumes.

Remember that the tax bill itself cannot be appealed. Only the value can, and the comparison the board cares about is market value against assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Who is paid the property tax in Bergen County?

The tax collector of your own municipality, not the county. All 70 towns run their own billing and payment methods, and the county board in Hackensack hears only assessment appeals.

By when must a Bergen County owner petition against an assessment?

By April 1 of the tax year, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of notices. Where a town revalued, the date is May 1.

Where can a Bergen County owner reach the Board of Taxation?

The office is at Two Bergen County Plaza, 1st Floor, in Hackensack, and the number is 201-336-6300. In person filing is accepted, though the county prefers online petitions.

What if a Bergen County owner skips the tax hearing?

The board can enter a judgment for lack of prosecution, which can bar a later appeal to the Tax Court. Adjournments are normally denied.

Can a Bergen County house sell while a tax quarter is unpaid?

Yes. Back taxes and interest are paid from the seller's share at closing, using the payoff the municipal collector supplies. Get that figure before you fix a closing date.

Which offices run property tax in Morris County

Property tax in Morris County is a shared job: a county board on one side and 39 town offices on the other. The Morris County Board of Taxation holds the county's records of taxable real estate, sets tax rates and equalization ratios, supervises the municipal assessors, reviews assessments and rules on appeals. Its mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900.

New Jersey leaves budgets to local government, and the state receives none of the property tax money. A town divides the dollars it must raise by the assessed value of everything taxable inside its borders, and that quotient is the general rate. Your bill equals the rate times your own assessment.

  • Your town's assessor sets the number printed on your notice.
  • The county board hears disputes about that number and publishes each town's rate.
  • The Morris County Clerk files the deed once the house closes.

Morris County homes and owners

Homeownership runs high and incomes are strong. About 524,251 people live here by the 2025 estimate, against 509,285 in 2020, spread over 193,245 households of 2.62 people on average. Roughly 91.1 percent of residents stayed in the same house for a year, which suggests that many sellers have owned for a long time.

Owners without a mortgage still carry $1,385 a month, and a large share of that is the tax bill and insurance. The land climbs from the flatter Passaic River valley suburbs in the east to hills in the west, and drainage differs between valley floor and ridge, so ask your town's office whether the lot sits near a mapped flood area before you set a price.

How to contest a Morris County assessment

Your petition has to reach the Morris County Board of Taxation by April 1, or May 1 in a town that just revalued or reassessed. Send form A-1 with the comparable sales sheet.

The board will call your value excessive only if it falls outside a set yardstick. After a revaluation, the yardstick is 100 percent of market value on the previous October 1. In other years, the town's common level range is the yardstick, set at plus or minus 15 percent around its average ratio.

  • Use arm's length sales dated before October 1.
  • Plan to appear in person, because the board runs no virtual hearings.
  • If the board's judgment disappoints you, the Tax Court of New Jersey is the next stop, with a 45 day clock.
  • An assessment over $1,000,000 gives the owner a choice to bypass the county board.
  • Added or omitted assessments use form AA-1, with direct Tax Court access above $750,000.

Relief that ends when you sell

All three of Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ are tied to a principal residence, so selling the house ends them for that address. An owner aged 65 or older may qualify for all three, and a renter qualifies for ANCHOR only. Each program has a yearly application window, so look for the next one on the state's relief page.

The state's home sale guide adds two cautions for movers. Say on the application that you moved after October 1, or the benefit can be lost. Anyone in Senior Freeze who buys another New Jersey home waits two years, instead of three, for a new base year.

Separate local deductions exist for seniors and disabled persons and for veteran owners, along with an exemption for a disabled veteran. Your town's tax office administers those, so ask whether the break on your Morris County house stops at closing.

If you are selling a house that a parent or spouse owned, ask the town's tax office whether a deduction from the former owner is still on the account. The new owner may need to file fresh forms, and the next bill will show the difference. Doing this before you list avoids a surprise after the buyer's lender has already priced the monthly payment from the old figure.

Keep a copy of any approval or denial letter you receive. The title company can ask for it, and it is the quickest way to show that a deduction or credit was dealt with properly before the deed changed hands.

What happens at the closing table

When the deed is recorded, the seller owes the state Realty Transfer Fee and files a GIT/REP form alongside it. A seller who remains a New Jersey resident signs GIT/REP-3, which means no deposit, and reports any gain on the NJ-1040 later. Rates sit on the state's Realty Transfer Fee page.

The Registry Department of the Morris County Clerk handles recording, from 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM, at 973-285-6130. Each land document goes in with a cover sheet and a cover letter giving the submitter's name and address, and the document itself carries a "Record & Return" or "Cancel & Return" note.

Get a payoff for any unpaid quarter from your town's tax office, and ask the closing attorney to prorate this year's bill. Those two figures decide what you net from a Morris County sale.

Selling with taxes owed

You can still sell a Morris County house that owes tax. Closing pays off the balance and any interest from the seller's share, which makes an accurate figure essential. The town tax office provides it, since the county neither bills nor collects.

  • Call the town tax office and have the payoff run through the day you close.
  • Pass the number to your closing attorney, who also splits the current year's bill between you and the buyer.
  • Confirm the block and lot number, which the deed package needs and the assessor can supply.
  • Mention a pending appeal to your attorney, since a lower value changes what the buyer sees on the record.

Older houses and estate sales often come to market needing a roof or a cleanout. Those houses draw fewer offers, which leaves the owner weighing an as-is sale against months of repairs. A house priced near the county's $582,500 typical value usually draws interest from buyers who already work nearby. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but the transfer fee, the deed recording and the tax payoff still happen at the same counters, so plan for them in either case.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I file a Morris County property tax appeal?

File with the Morris County Board of Taxation, using Form A-1 and the comparable sales form. The board's mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900, and hearings take place in person.

What is the deadline for a Morris County tax appeal?

April 1 is the usual receipt date, and May 1 replaces it after a town revaluation or reassessment. Since the board wants the petition in hand by then, send it well ahead of time.

Does Morris County bill my property tax?

No, your municipality bills and collects it. The county board sets rates and equalization ratios and hears appeals, while your town's tax office issues the bill and supplies payoff figures at a sale.

Can a $1.2 million assessment bypass the county board?

Yes, you may take an assessment above $1,000,000 straight to the Tax Court of New Jersey. The same April 1 or May 1 receipt date governs that filing.

Who pays the transfer fee on a Morris County sale?

The seller pays at recording. A graduated percent fee also falls on the seller if the price goes above $1,000,000.

Which offices touch a property tax bill in Ocean County?

A house in Ocean County is valued by the town assessor and billed by the town collector. At the county level, the Board of Taxation hears challenges to assessments. Property tax questions go to the tax collector of the municipality where the home sits, not to the county.

The county has 33 municipalities, from Lakewood and Toms River to small shore boroughs such as Harvey Cedars and Mantoloking. Each one bills on its own schedule inside the state framework, so the first call for any Ocean County seller is the collector in the town that holds the parcel.

Ocean County housing snapshot

Ocean County has grown faster than any other New Jersey county since 2020, reaching an estimated 673,746 people in 2025, a 5.7% gain. Owners live in 80.7% of homes. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $398,400, and median household income is $89,863.

Residents 65 or older make up 24.0% of the county, so many sellers hold senior benefits tied to the house, and a buyer should know which ones end at sale. Assessments vary widely from town to town. A bayfront bungalow in Brick, a retirement-community home in Manchester and a Lakewood multifamily house can carry very different assessments and very different bills.

What happens when an Ocean County installment is paid late?

The year splits into four installments that fall due on the first day of February, May, August and November. Interest on a late installment is set by town resolution, up to 8% annually on the first $1,500 owed and up to 18% annually on whatever exceeds it.

A town can also allow a ten day grace period before interest starts. Whether a given Ocean County town allows one is a local decision, so ask that town's collector before counting on a grace window. Unpaid balances can end up in a tax sale. Under R.S. 54:5-19, a town may run an accelerated sale for amounts still unpaid on the 11th day of the eleventh month of the fiscal year. How an Ocean County assessment appeal works

The Ocean County Board of Taxation takes petitions through April 1. A town that finished a citywide revaluation or reassessment gets until May 1 instead, and late-mailed assessment notices stretch the window to 45 days after the bulk mailing. A petition mailed on the last day but received the next one is late, because the board closes at 4:30 p.m.

  • File one petition per parcel and serve a copy on the town assessor and the municipal clerk.
  • Fees scale with assessed value: $5 below $150,000, $25 up to $500,000, $100 up to $1 million and $150 beyond that, by check payable to the Ocean County Treasurer.
  • Deliver up to five comparable sales, plus any appraisal, no later than a week before the hearing.
  • Be current on all taxes through the first quarter of the tax year, as N.J.S.A. 54:3-27 requires.

Only the assessment is on the table. The bill itself comes from budgets, and the assessment is presumed correct until you prove otherwise. A typical hearing begins at nine in the morning. A no-show without a written postponement ends in dismissal, and that kind of dismissal cannot be taken to Tax Court. Either side can carry a county judgment to the Tax Court of New Jersey by filing a complaint within 45 days of mailing. Left alone, the judgment is frozen: it binds the assessor for the assessment year and the next two.

  • ANCHOR gives relief to owners and renters who live in the property as their main home and meet income limits.
  • Local deductions for qualifying veteran, senior and disabled owners come through the town assessor, and a dispute over a denied deduction can be filed with the county board at no fee.

If you hold any of these, tell the buyer's side early. Some benefits depend on living in the home as a main residence, so they stop mattering to you once you sell.

Deeds are filed with the Ocean County Clerk. At the Clerk's Office a deed costs $45 for its first page and $10 per added page, a mortgage costs $35 to start, and a missing cover sheet adds $20. Payment is by cash, check or escrow account, and checks over $10,000 must be certified.

Ahead of closing, request a tax search and payoff letter from the town collector, and ask the assessor whether a pending appeal, added assessment or deduction affects the next bill. Old tax sale certificates are recorded at the Clerk's Office as well, at $35, and must be redeemed or cancelled for clean title.

Where do I pay Ocean County property tax?

Payment goes to your own town's tax collector. Tax questions are directed to the collector for the town that holds the parcel.

When must an Ocean County appeal be filed?

April 1 is the standard cutoff. Towns that just revalued or reassessed get May 1, and notices mailed late stretch either date to 45 days after the bulk mailing. The board closes at 4:30 p.m.

Can I appeal my tax bill in Ocean County?

No. Only the assessed value can be appealed, since taxes come from the budget process. You need sales or an appraisal showing market value on the prior October 1, enough to overcome the presumption that the assessment is right.

What is the filing fee for an Ocean County appeal?

The fee runs from $5 to $150 depending on assessed value. There is no fee to contest the denial of a veteran, senior or disabled deduction.

Can I sell an Ocean County house that has back taxes?

Yes. Arrears and interest come off the seller's side of the closing statement, so ask the town collector for a payoff figure first. A tax sale certificate, if one exists, has to be redeemed before title is clear.

Who handles property tax in Essex County

Its phone is 973-395-8525 and its website is essexcountynjtaxboard.org, where you will find appeal forms, tax rates, the equalization table, deduction forms and a contact list for every town's assessor and collector.

Bills combine school, municipal and county levies, so two similar houses in different Essex towns can land with quite different totals. The board posts pie charts showing how each town's tax dollar is divided, which is a quick way to see where your own money goes.

  • Assessor: sets the assessed value and handles deductions and exemptions.

Essex County housing at a glance

Essex County is crowded: about 896,000 people on 126.09 square miles of land, with Newark as the county seat. Typical home value for 2020 to 2024 is $524,100, and median gross rent is $1,531. Only 44.9% of households own their home, so renters fill most of the housing and many sales involve a tenant already in place. The east side is anchored by Newark Liberty International Airport, Port Newark and Newark Penn Station. The west side holds the Oranges, Montclair, Verona and the Caldwells. Appeal deadline

Essex County follows the state calendar. The county board must have your petition in hand on April 1, or by the 45th day after the town finishes mailing assessment notices, whichever is later. Where a town has completed a municipal-wide revaluation or reassessment, the deadline is May 1. A postmark earns nothing here, and a late petition is thrown out.

If April 1 or May 1 falls on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, the last day moves to the following working day. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 may skip the county board and file in the Tax Court of New Jersey, with the same dates. The board's public schedule of meetings and tax appeal hearings is on its website.

How to file an Essex County appeal

Start with the state's Form A-1 and its comparable sales sheet, and file the original with the Essex County Tax Board. The board's site lists its current appeal forms and reminders, and the Division of Taxation has the same forms.

  • Build your case on market value as of October 1 of the pretax year. The appeal covers the assessed value alone.
  • List up to five comparable sales, giving block, lot, price and deed date for each. The board will not take other homes' assessments as comparables.
  • Check your town's average ratio on the equalization table. If the ratio of assessed to true value falls outside a band of 15 percent around the average, the board adjusts the value using that average ratio.
  • Serve a copy on your municipal assessor and clerk.
  • Attend the hearing yourself or send an attorney, unless you chose a summary hearing on written evidence.

If the board turns you down, the Tax Court in Trenton takes a complaint filed within 45 days of the judgment. A board judgment holds for the year and the two after it unless a revaluation or added assessment changes the picture.

What happens at a tax board hearing?

You pick the format on the petition: an in-person hearing, a virtual hearing if the county offers one, or a summary hearing decided only on the papers you send. A summary hearing means you cannot explain your comparables aloud, so every sale you rely on has to be clearly like your house. Homeowners may speak for themselves, while an LLC, trust or corporation needs a New Jersey attorney unless the property's prior-year tax was under $25,000.

Installments and late interest

Essex owners pay in four quarterly installments, due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Many towns give a 10-day grace window after each date. Nothing stops you from selling a house that still has tax owing. The back tax, interest and any lien get paid out of your proceeds at closing, so get the figures early.

  • Confirm whether the water or sewer account is separate from the tax account.
  • Pay the installment that falls during your closing window, or make sure the title company withholds it.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but the tax payoff still has to be settled before the deed is recorded, so the collector's letter matters just as much.

Relief programs and deductions

The state's fiscal year 2027 budget pays for Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ. Application windows run on a yearly cycle, so check the Division of Taxation page for the next one. The municipal assessor handles the $250 deductions for qualified veteran, senior and disabled owners, and the full exemption for a 100 percent disabled veteran. The Essex board lists those forms online.

Your status on October 1 of the year before the tax year decides eligibility, and the senior and disabled deduction carries an income ceiling of $10,000 that leaves out certain Social Security and pension income. If a town denies a deduction, you can appeal that denial to the county board without paying a filing fee. If you are selling, ask the assessor how a deduction on the house is handled once the deed changes hands.

The deadline moves from April 1 to May 1 for that year. The board and your municipal assessor can confirm whether your town qualifies.

Is a late Essex County appeal ever accepted?

No. The petition has to be received by the end of business on the deadline date, and the board dismisses late filings.

Do I keep paying tax while an appeal is open?

Yes. You must stay current through the first quarter at least, and the board may relax that rule when justice requires.

Can an Essex County house sell with tax still owed?

Yes. The unpaid tax, interest and any lien are cleared from the seller's money at the table, so request a payoff letter from the municipal collector first.

The Chapter 123 ratio and your assessment

The best evidence is recent arm's-length sales of comparable homes, supplied within the board's timeline. Sales must support the value as of October 1 of the year before the appeal. Sales outside the sampling window or between related parties can be disqualified. Sale records are available from your assessor, so confirm with that office that any sale you pick is counted as usable.

  • Notices go out at least 10 days ahead, and hearings run from April through August, Tuesday through Friday.
  • Hearings run online, with a call-in option. Adjournments are rarely granted.

Prepare a short written summary listing each comparable sale, its date and why it matches your house. The board decides on the evidence submitted, so put your explanation of why the comparables fit your house in writing instead of saving it for a conversation.

Selling with property tax owed

A seller with unpaid taxes can still close. The balance is settled from proceeds at the closing table, and the town's payoff statement tells the closing agent exactly what to send. Interest keeps running until then, so ask the collector for a figure that stays good through the closing date, and keep the written statement with your closing papers.

Contact the collector in the town where the house sits and ask for a written payoff. Each of the 21 municipalities runs its own office with its own phone line, and the county board lists the collector contacts for each town. The assessor in the same town can tell you whether an added or omitted assessment is pending for new work on the house.

If you think the value is wrong, remember the filing windows are fixed and hearings run April through August. Ask the board about any petition already on file, and tell the buyer's side about it before closing. Gather your tax bills, your sale contract and any assessment notice, so the closing agent can settle the balance out of your proceeds. Also ask your attorney whether the sale contract should say who keeps any refund if an appeal succeeds after closing, since a reduced assessment can produce a credit that someone has to claim.

Does Union County itself send my tax bill?

No. Each of the 21 municipalities bills its own taxes through its own tax collector. The county supervises assessment through the Board of Taxation in Westfield.

What is the Union County Board of Taxation phone number?

908-527-4775. The office is at 300 North Avenue East, Westfield, open Monday to Friday from 8:00 am to 4:00 pm, and it can be reached by email at uctaxboard@ucnj.org.

Can my real estate agent file my tax appeal?

No. Only an owner or an attorney may file. Agents and appraisers cannot file or sign an appeal for a taxpayer.

Can I appeal if my property taxes are behind?

It can be dismissed. Taxes and municipal charges must be paid up through the first quarter of the current year when an appeal is filed.

When does a Union County tax appeal hearing take place?

Between April and August, Tuesday through Friday, online with a call-in option. Hearing notices are mailed at least 10 days before the date, and evidence is due seven calendar days beforehand.

Who does what on property tax in Camden County

Three layers share the work in Camden County. The town assessor sets value, the town collector sends the bill and takes the payment, and the Camden County Board of Taxation settles disputes over value. The board sits at 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood, has public hours on weekdays from 9 to 4 and a phone line at 856-225-5238.

  • A change of name or mailing address is requested in writing at the municipal assessor's office.

Camden County housing in brief

Camden County stretches along the Delaware River directly across from Philadelphia. It has 36 municipalities, from dense river towns to the wooded suburbs near Voorhees and Cherry Hill, and an estimated 535,799 residents. A typical home is valued near $287,100, owners occupy about 64.7 percent of households, and the middle household earns $88,755 a year. The PATCO Speedline runs from Philadelphia through Camden to Lindenwold, with stops at Woodcrest, Westmont and Collingswood, and that rail access draws commuters. The land is low and flat, and an aging storm drain system leaves parts of the county exposed to flooding, which buyers and inspectors look at closely.

Appeal deadlines

Petitions are accepted from the time assessment notices go out until the 4 p.m. close on April 1, or the 45th day after the town finishes its notice mailing, whichever is later. A petition still in the mail at that hour is late. Postmarks are ignored, and anything late is thrown out.

Towns that have just finished a revaluation or reassessment get a one-month extension to May 1. The board's website names the towns in that position for the current cycle, and a deadline falling on a Sunday or legal holiday slides to the following working day. Bills for added or omitted assessments, which come from new construction or an error on the tax list, follow their own December 1 rule.

How to file with the county board

Petitions can be sent through the board's online portal, by post, or delivered by hand, and hearings run in a virtual format alongside the Blackwood meeting room. Online filing works best in Chrome, Safari or Firefox, and the paper form is on the board's forms page.

  • File one petition and pay one fee per parcel: $5 when assessed value is under $150,000, $25 up to $500,000, $100 up to $1,000,000, and $150 beyond that.
  • Give your town's assessor and clerk their own copies.
  • Use up to five comparable sales, with block, lot, sale price and deed date. Comparable assessments do not count as evidence.
  • Keep paying installments during the case, at the very least through the first quarter, unless the board eases that requirement.

Only assessed value can be appealed. To win, show the house's market value on the October 1 before the tax year. If the board lowers your value, the judgment is held in place for that year and the next two unless something such as a town revaluation changes it.

Can a Camden County house sell while tax is still owed?

Yes, though the debt does not vanish at sale. It stays attached to the property until somebody pays. Once the grace period ends, interest runs back to the due date at 8 percent a year on the first $1,500 owed and 18 percent a year on the remainder.

If a town sells a tax lien on your property, the house cannot be sold until the lien is redeemed. A buyer who holds the lien can start foreclosure in state court if it stays open for two years. Ask the town collector for a written payoff, with interest worked out to a named date, before you sign a contract.

  • Pass the latest bill to the buyer or title company.
  • Check sewer and water accounts separately, because many towns bill them apart from the tax.
  • Several quarters behind? Ask for the payoff early so the closing agent has time to plan.

Three state relief programs, Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ, are funded in the fiscal year 2027 budget for owners and renters. The Division of Taxation's relief page carries the current application window, so check it each year.

Your municipal assessor handles the state deductions: $250 for a qualifying veteran, $250 for seniors and disabled owners under the income limit, and a full exemption where a service-connected disability is rated 100 percent permanent and total. Request the current application from your assessor, and let your closing agent know about any deduction so the proration comes out right.

Start with paperwork. Pull your latest tax bill, your assessment notice and any sewer or water statements. Ask the collector for a written payoff and the assessor for your property record card, then check the card against the house as it really is. Errors in square footage or room count are a common reason for an appeal.

Short on time? A cash sale avoids the bank appraisal and most repairs. The tax payoff, the lien check and the deduction proration still happen at closing, so ordering them early keeps the date firm.

Also ask about sewer and water bills, since many towns send those separately, and about any added or omitted assessment bill that may follow new construction. Keep copies of every notice. If a hearing is scheduled, put the date on your calendar and send your comparable sales to the board, the assessor and the clerk at least seven days ahead.

Frequently asked questions

Which office takes a Camden County assessment appeal?

The board at 509 Lakeland Road, Blackwood, NJ 08012, accepts petitions online, by mail or at the counter. Call 856-225-5238 with questions, and give your town assessor and clerk a copy.

Does the April 1 appeal date ever change?

Yes. Towns that completed a revaluation or reassessment use May 1 instead. In every case the petition has to reach the board before it closes for the day on the final date.

Does an appeal lower my tax bill right away?

No. You keep paying your installments, at least through the first quarter, while the case is pending. A reduction in value carries into later bills and any overpayment is dealt with after judgment.

Can I sell with back taxes owed?

Yes. Closing pays off tax, interest and any lien from the seller's proceeds. Get the written payoff from your town collector before choosing a closing date.

Who sets Camden County tax rates?

Each town's rate comes from the combined school, municipal, county and any special district levies divided by the town's total assessed value. The county board of taxation sets the rate, and your municipal collector bills it.

Middlesex County and its towns

A house in a Raritan Bay town such as South Amboy and one in a Route 1 corridor township such as South Brunswick are billed by different municipalities and school districts, even though the same county board rules on their appeals.

Offices that run property tax

Middlesex County does not send most homeowners a tax bill. In each of the twenty-five towns, a local assessor values property and a local collector sends the bill, and the county tax board supervises that work and hears appeals. Planning an appeal? The April 1 date (May 1 after a revaluation) still applies, and the first quarter's taxes and municipal charges normally have to be paid for it to move forward. Calling the wrong office wastes a week, so match the question to the desk. A lien sold on your parcel is a claim that must be paid, with interest, before the title is clear. Get the redemption amount from the collector in writing. The title company will also ask for the block and lot number printed on your bill, so keep it handy.

Do this before you list, since buyers and their lenders look at the bill on record when they estimate monthly costs.

Which offices handle property tax in Passaic County?

Passaic County splits the work between its 16 municipalities and one county board. Each town assessor values property and each town collector bills it. The Passaic County Board of Taxation, created by legislation in 1909, certifies assessments, equalizes values for county tax purposes, prepares the abstract of ratables, certifies municipal tax rates and hears assessment appeals.

  • Town assessor: valuation, deductions, added and omitted assessments.
  • Town collector: bills, payments and tax payoff letters for a sale.

A Passaic County seller should begin with the collector in the house's own town, because the county board neither bills nor collects.

Passaic County at a glance

The county is small and dense. Its 186.01 square miles of land hold about 2,818 people per square mile as of the 2020 Census, and the 2025 estimate is 531,624 residents in 186,341 housing units. Paterson is the county seat and holds more than 30% of the population. The county was created on February 7, 1837 from parts of Bergen and Essex counties.

Owners live in 53.1% of homes, the median home is worth $459,500 and the median household earns $87,522. Within one county a seller might hold a two-family house, a rental building or a hillside single-family home, and the tax picture differs for each.

The southeastern half is flat or gently hilly along the Passaic and Pompton Rivers, while the northwest is rugged highland, with West Milford covering 80.32 square miles, more than 40% of the county's area. The lowest ground, about 20 feet above sea level, lies along the Passaic River in Clifton. A seller in a river town does well to gather repair records and any flood history before the first showing, and to ask the town building department about open permits before listing.

Appeal deadlines

Wait for the assessment card before filing, which means filing from February 1, and get a regular petition in by April 1. A town that has just revalued or reassessed gets until May 1; for 2026 that town was Paterson. Added and omitted assessments have their own later deadline.

How does a Passaic County appeal work once it is filed?

What can be challenged is the assessed value. The rate cannot, and the owner must show what the house was worth the prior October 1.

  • Bring recent sales of similar homes near the October 1 date, with photographs and a property record card from the town assessor.
  • Above $1,000,000 of assessed value, the owner may skip the board and file in state Tax Court.
  • A dissatisfied owner has 45 days after the judgment to go to Tax Court.
  • Added or omitted assessment bills are generally mailed in October and payable November 1, and an appeal of one must be filed before December 1.

State rules on added assessments say that work finished after October 1 is valued as of the next month's first day and taxed for the whole months left in that year. A seller who built a new deck, a finished basement or an extension should expect the assessor to notice.

What happens to unpaid Passaic County property tax?

Each town sets its own late interest within the state ceiling. Debt left open at the close of the fiscal year leads to a standard tax sale the year after, and debt still open on November 11 of the fiscal year can lead to an accelerated sale. A town may leave a property out of the sale if the owner is paying a signed plan in equal monthly installments that clears the debt within five years.

A town may also add a year-end penalty, capped at 6%, to any delinquency above $10,000. Interest runs daily, so a seller who owes should ask the collector for the exact figure on the closing date.

Relief programs run through the state, and one application covers Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ. Call the Division of Taxation for the next filing cycle.

Recording fees and the transfer tax

Deeds and mortgages are recorded by the Passaic County Clerk. The Registry fee list charges $45 for the first page of a deed plus $10 per extra page, $35 to open a mortgage, and $20 for a notice of settlement naming two parties. A mortgage cancellation is $25, and an inheritance tax waiver is $15. Discharge papers for a veteran record at no fee, and a certified copy of a recorded document costs $10 for the first page and $2 for each page after.

The same schedule carries a realty transfer tax table. In the bracket for prices up to $350,000, the first $150,000 is taxed at $4.00 per $1,000, the next $50,000 at $6.70, and the rest up to $350,000 at $7.80. Above $350,000 the rates start at $5.80 per $1,000 and climb in steps to $12.10 per $1,000 above $1,000,000. Senior citizen rates are lower. Your closing agent will confirm which column applies.

Steps to take before you sell

Start with the town collector and ask for a payoff letter. It fixes the number the closing agent remits, interest included. Also ask whether a tax sale certificate has been issued on the parcel, since one has to be redeemed before title is clear.

Then check with the assessor about added or omitted assessments, and with the building department about open permits. Both can change what a buyer's attorney asks for at the table.

Individual owners may represent themselves in an appeal at the county board, while business entities other than sole proprietorships need an attorney. If you plan to appeal and sell in the same year, tell your closing attorney so the filing is handled at closing.

A cash buyer buying as-is skips repairs and a lender's appraisal, but the payoff and recording steps stay the same. The collector's letter and the clerk's recording fees are what the closing date depends on.

Because the county is split into 16 towns, the order of calls matters. Phone the collector in your own town for the balance, the assessor in the same town for any pending change, and only then the county clerk about recording. A seller who skips the first call can learn about a lien from the title company late in the process, when little time is left to fix it.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Passaic County Board of Taxation?

It is at 930 Riverview Drive, Suite 250, Totowa, NJ 07512, and the phone is (973) 720-7399. Appeal hearings are held in Suite 200 at the same address, starting at 9 a.m.

When is the Passaic County tax appeal deadline?

A regular petition is due April 1. A revalued or reassessed town gets May 1, and added or omitted assessments close December 1. Wait for the assessment card before filing.

Who pays property tax in Passaic County, the county or the town?

You pay your town's tax collector. The county board certifies and hears appeals, but the town bills and collects for municipal, school and county levies together.

Can I appeal a Passaic County assessment on my own?

Yes. Individual owners may represent themselves at the county board, while business entities other than sole proprietorships need an attorney. Properties assessed above $1,000,000 may bypass the board.

Can I sell a Passaic County house with tax owing?

Yes. The collector's payoff letter fixes the number the closing agent remits, interest included. Also ask the town whether a tax sale certificate has been issued on the parcel.
